scoreNote: Strong (5): attacks the reason by showing new leadership is not the surest path to success, then the claim by showing a universal five-year limit would squander experience, and proposes renewal through accountability rather than automatic turnover.

sentences.text: Fresh leadership can breathe new life into a tired institution — but does that make pushing out every leader every five years a law worth passing?

The claim says it does, holding that those in power in any field should step down after five years, on the reason that the surest path to success for any enterprise is revitalization through new leadership.

Both the claim and its reason go too far: forced turnover in every field would waste expertise as often as it renews things, and revitalization through new leadership, though sometimes valuable, is hardly the surest path to success.

sections.role: Body — The reason overstates new leadership

sentences.text: Consider first the reason, which mistakes one occasional benefit for a universal law.
New leaders can indeed bring fresh energy and ideas, and an enterprise that has grown stale sometimes needs exactly that.
But to call new leadership the surest path to success is plainly false, since success far more often depends on competence, sound strategy, and steady execution than on novelty for its own sake.
A capable leader who has mastered her role typically serves an enterprise better than an untested newcomer, and replacing her on schedule is as likely to interrupt success as to renew it.
Stability and mastery, not constant reshuffling, are what most successful enterprises actually run on.
Revitalization is one path to success among many, not the surest.
However, the claim built on this shaky reason is shakier still.
Forcing every leader in every field out after five years would throw away the accumulated knowledge, relationships, and judgment that take far longer than that to build.
A surgeon, a scientist, a teacher, or a seasoned manager often reaches her most valuable years only after a decade, and a rigid five-year limit would expel her at her peak.
The constant churn would mean perpetual inexperience, with institutions forever relearning what their departed leaders already knew.
A rule that sacrifices experience to a theory of perpetual renewal would weaken the very enterprises it means to strengthen.

sections.role: Body — A better path to renewal

sentences.text: Moreover, where renewal genuinely matters, there are better ways to secure it than expelling everyone on a timer.
An enterprise can refresh itself through new ideas, regular evaluation, and the steady promotion of talent without discarding its most capable people every five years.

The real danger is not long service but entrenched, unaccountable power, and that is met by accountability — review, competition, and the freedom to remove poor leaders — not by removing good ones automatically.
Keep the leaders who are succeeding, renew those who are failing, and let performance rather than the calendar decide.
Renewal is best pursued by judgment, not by a blanket expiry date stamped on competence.
In conclusion, both the claim and its reason should be rejected.

New leadership is sometimes revitalizing but is far from the surest path to success, and a universal five-year limit would squander expertise across every field, so enterprises are better served by keeping capable leaders, removing failing ones, and seeking renewal through accountability rather than automatic turnover.
Replace leaders who have failed, not leaders who have merely lasted.
